item.title: Fighting manipulated fertiliser prices
item.description:
By Neil Ray

Transplantation of Aman seedlings has started in several areas of the country but farmers, according to a report carried in the FE, are forced to pay Tk 3.0-12 in excess for each kilogram of fertiliser on the rates fixed by the government. Agriculture Minister Mohammed Aminur Rashid claims there is no shortage of any type of fertiliser needed for Aman cultivation. The supply-line disruption is the result of a 'planned conspiracy', the minister observes. Clearly, it is a management problem. 

Traders in this country take advantage of any loophole in the system of marketing of essentials. In the case of fertiliser distribution, abolition of the retail dealer arrangement under the recently announced Integrated Policy on Fertiliser Dealer Appointment and Fertiliser Distribution 2025 (revised), may have contributed to the disorder in fertiliser distribution. The dealership structure has shaped into a hereditary business and the new policy announced by the government, according to market insiders, will not bring about a desirable change in the system. 

Aman season accounts for the second-highest application of fertiliser to the tune of 2.0 million tonnes out of 6.0-6.5 million tonnes required for the country. The share of annual production of Aman crop is 38-39 per cent of the total rice yield. This means that this cereal needs comparatively far less fertiliser than Boro which requires the highest amount of fertiliser. Now if smooth distribution cannot be ensured, costs on account of this essential input increase and many farmers cannot afford it. But timely application of fertiliser is a must for good harvest. 

If a farmer has to pay Tk 12 more than the fixed rate for a kilogram of fertiliser, the cost escalates to a staggering figure on a 50 kilo sack. Other inputs like irrigation, if needed, are likely to be costlier as well. At a time when diesel used for pumping machines is costlier and electricity supply is uncertain in rural areas, manipulating fertiliser supply line for profit can have deleterious impacts on production of this rice variety. This is criminal. If rice production suffers on account of manmade crisis despite adequate stock of the input, those responsible for the artificial shortage should be brought to book. 

So, the concerned minister's job is not just to point out the manipulation of fertiliser market but to address the problem before the disruption of the supply chain severely affects Aman cultivation. Identifying the perpetrators for awarding them due punishment can be a deterrent to this crime. The Department of Agricultural Extension (DAE) can monitor the distribution process and identify where things go wrong. The dual arrangement of distribution of fertiliser by the Bangladesh Chemical Industries Corporation (BCIC) and the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation (BADC) does not help the cause. Accusation and counter-accusation by the two agencies for additional profit making indicate that the rivalry between them is far from healthy.  They could inspire their respective dealers to compete with each other in the performance of distribution. When staple production is involved, there is no point allowing room for taking advantage of any missing link in between supply and application in the field. 

The good news is that the Bangladesh Fertiliser Association has instructed its district committees to monitor dealers and retailers and warned that those overcharging for sale of fertiliser may lose their registration. But dishonest dealers and retailers have their own mechanism to realise extra profits. Harassed farmers are forced to pay extra money while receipt shows the sale of fertiliser at the official rate. This calls for stricter monitoring and launching a campaign among farmers to report any malpractice by dealers and retailers. If farmers collectively oppose any manoeuvring by dealers and retailers, the latter's designs can be thwarted. In fact, if farmers' groups or organisations are formed to fight the malpractices resorted to by dealers and their agents, the move can yield positive results. Complemented by official monitoring, farmers' resistance can bring an end to illegal profit making by dealers.

item.title: 'Pink Bus' and the gender politics: Structural development or attitudinal shift?
item.description:
By ISHRAT JAHAN PROMI

The recent introduction of women-only 'Pink Buses' on Dhaka's streets has quickly become one of the most discussed public agendas.

The government deserves recognition for finally taking a step towards creating a safer commuting space for women in the capital after years of concern over their safety on public transport. Yet an important question remains: are structural interventions alone sufficient to reduce gender-based disparity in Bangladesh? Or is there much more to untangle within the deeply rooted stereotypes that continue to operate across our social institutions? 

The answer, I believe, is clear. Gender-based inequality cannot be eliminated simply by creating separate buses, buildings, roads, or other physical spaces.

Structural change matters, but social institutions must also change the attitudes and practices that reproduce inequality. 

We do not need to look far for an example. Just a day after the inauguration of the Pink Buses, my social-media newsfeed was flooded with news reports, photocards, memes, and videos presenting a wide range of reactions.

What struck me, however, was an unsettling trend: even formal news organisations appeared to be participating in a competition to capitalise on misogyny. 

This is particularly unfortunate because newspapers and news organisations are often considered reflections of society. Yet some of them continue to reinforce misogynistic attitudes through how stories are framed.

One leading national daily, for instance, published a photocard  with the headline: "She drove the Pink Bus onto the flyover; a male driver came to the rescue." 

The question is simple. Of all the road accidents and traffic violations that have taken place over the years, how often have newspapers highlighted that an incident was caused specifically by a male driver?

I would argue they rarely do. When a man makes a driving mistake, his gender is generally irrelevant to the story. But when a woman makes a similar mistake, her gender suddenly becomes part of the headline. 

Another prominent daily interviewed some male drivers to ask whether allowing women to take the steering wheel was a worthwhile decision. The framing almost suggested that something extraordinary or even dangerous was happening simply because women were driving buses. 

It creates the impression that people are waiting, popcorn in hand, for the slightest mistake by a female driver so that it can be amplified, ridiculed, and used to validate pre-existing misogynistic beliefs. 

Why does this happen? Why, instead of encouraging a potentially groundbreaking initiative, do some sections of the media instinctively frame it through skepticism, ridicule, or gendered suspicion?

One possible explanation lies in the logic of the attention-driven digital economy and the commercialisation of misogyny.

Research by Yi Chen, Fei Li, and Marcel Preuss, affiliated with Cornell University and the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill, develops an economic model of algorithmic attention to explain how digital platforms allocate user attention and how this process connects to economic incentives. Their work helps us understand how competition for attention can influence the kinds of content that gain visibility in digital environments. 

Digitally transformed news media are not exempt from this logic. News organisations increasingly operate in an environment in which clicks, comments, shares, views, and other forms of engagement carry measurable economic value.

Under these conditions, sensational or provocative framing may become commercially attractive precisely because it generates stronger reactions. 

At the same time, the growing use of clickbait headlines in online journalism reflects pressure to attract audiences in an intensely competitive digital environment. Taken together, these trends raise an important possibility that belittles, sexualises, ridicules, or controversially portrays women.  

Another hidden reality is the limited presence of women journalists in newsrooms. 

Throughout my professional journey, while conducting more than a dozen trainings on gender equality across nearly all eight divisions of Bangladesh, I have repeatedly asked participants how many women work in the newsrooms of the local news offices.

The number rarely rises above two or three. The situation in local newspapers is even more alarming; in many cases, having even one woman journalist in the newsroom can seem fortunate. 

This absence matters. Keeping women largely absent from the spaces where news is selected, processed, framed, and presented creates conditions in which a predominantly male discourse can continue with little internal challenge.

The lack of women in decision-making and editorial processes can therefore make inclusive representation even more difficult to achieve. 

The Pink Bus initiative should consequently encourage us to think beyond the buses themselves. 

Creating a separate transport service for women may address an immediate structural problem. Still, it cannot by itself dismantle the social attitudes that make such interventions necessary in the first place.

The government, media institutions, and wider society must begin to recognise women as independent social agents rather than as exceptions whose actions require constant gendered scrutiny.

What Bangladesh needs is not structural development alone, but ethical, institutional, and collective transformation. 

An inclusive Bangladesh will not be built simply by putting women behind the wheel of a pink bus. It will also require changing the social and media environment that waits for those women to make a mistake and then turns that mistake into a spectacle. 

The author is a Lecturer in the Department of Mass Communication and Journalism at  Bangladesh University of Professionals (BUP). She has also been actively engaged as a trainer on gender equality, facilitating sessions with hundreds of youth. She can be reached at [email protected]

item.title: Introducing dCash
item.description:
By Md. Mashiur Rahman

Digital Cash (dCash) is a digitally transferable payment instrument issued against receivables to facilitate short-term financing, typically for periods ranging from 30 to 120 days, with a maximum tenor of one year. dCash is designed to support the purchase and sale of goods and services by enabling purchasers to make payments through the transfer of digital units issued by banks, financial institutions, or fintech companies. The primary purpose of dCash is to facilitate settlement of payments arising from credit sales. It enables seamless digital transactions in both Business-to-Consumer (B2C) and Business-to-Business (B2B) markets, providing an efficient, secure and transferable digital payment mechanism for commercial transactions.

Description of business idea

As reported by IDLC Finance Ltd. the current market size of supply chain finance is approximately BDT 40 billion (4,000 crore) including banks and non-bank financial institutions. But, it has the potential to grow as the opportunities are huge. Moreover, the global market volume of supply chain finance was worth about USD 5.70 billion in 2025. Its shows that there is more room for work in the area of supply chain financing. In view of the scarcity of both deposit and capital for supply chain financing companies and the short time financing i.e. duration of finance is less than one (01) year, an innovative product like DigitalCash holds out immense potential in revolutionising transactions in our country.

Based on digital cash, a fintech company/bank/finance company can share digit/point favouring the suppliers of goods on behalf of customers for a short term backed by 100 per cent or more receivables. During the period the fintech company can charge a maximum of 0.50 per cent per quarter service charge against the point/digit instead of regular interest rate (around 15.00 per cent). The example below will make the issue more clear:

For credit sales of Tk. 100, the company will issue 100 points/digits in favour of the seller on behalf of the buyer. The seller can then distribute these points to their suppliers, who in turn can further distribute them for purchasing purposes. If the credit duration is 90 days, after this period, the holder of the points can submit them to the company and receive Tk.100 in cash. The company will recover the Tk.100 from the initial buyer. In case the buyer is unable to make the payment due to unsold goods, they can take a loan from the fintech company against hypothecation of goods, post-dated cheque, guarantee, etc.

To manage the process and maintain a balance, a blockchain or digital ledger system can be developed. This system will mitigate short-term liquidity crises and ensure more business opportunities through reducing the cost of fund (only commission instead of high interest), that will ultimately create jobs in national and international markets. Here a fintech, a bank or a non-bank institution will only develop an eco-system for the supply chain financing company/fintech.

Product or service description

Digital Cash (dCash)

This is a new type of cash transferrable digitally and issued against receivables for short time financing i.e. for 30 days to 120 days and /or a maximum of one year. The dCash can be used for buying and selling of goods and services where the purchaser will make payment through transferring digits. For safety and balancing of dCash, a digital blockchain system under the control of the issuing company will be developed. However, in coming days if government approves, the issuing company may issue a digital cash note with an expiry date and a hologram. The digital cash always have an expiry date forecasting a receivable cash conversion cycle. If the first purchaser of goods/service fails to make payment on maturity, then the financing company/dCash issuing company will make payment favouring the bearer of dCash on maturity i.e. dCash issuing company will take the credit risk of the first purchaser and, if suitable, the dCash company may go for insurance against the credit risk. The dCash is primarily to be utilized for payment against credit sales where users can be Business to Consumer and/or Business to Business.

Market analysis

The proposed dCash will support the business enterprise to purchase goods in advance on credit and run the business during the credit period by selling without short-term bank loan. As such, the seller of the goods will not pay any interest to the supply chain financing company but only service charge which is very minimum, maybe a maximum of 0.50% per quarter while the present interest rate for a private company is about 15.00 per cent per annum and 3.75 per cent per quarter.

This shows that costing of production and/or sales will be downgraded rapidly but the government can earn in the form of Value Added Tax (VAT) as well as direct tax as more business will be done for lower costing and consequently lower price. This will ultimately generate employment as well.

Marketing and promotion plans

We assume that marketing means mitigating customer needs profitably and for achieving the marketing goals, it needs people to people networking and also organizational networking. The proposed dCash will work as an ecosystem of existing supply chain financing companies already having a customer base. Moreover, using social media, electronic media and print media the supply chain financing company will speed up its publicity. Moreover, as this is an innovative and easily doable idea, the news media will cover news which will ultimately aid the promotional campaign too.

Competitor analysis

The existing supply chain company will not utilize the proposed technology for mitigation of any liquidity crisis as they may not know how to utilize the system. As such, it will face no major competition in marketing the proposed dCash.

(i) Risk: There will be a challenge for credit checking of first purchaser or finding the credit history of first purchaser.

Risk Mitigation: In this case, the bank/ fintech company will do the KYC exercise as per prescribed format and also obtain required documents for the purpose of KYC.

(ii) Risk: There is a default risk from the initial buyer's side.

Risk Mitigation: Hypothecation of goods and/or security cheque/insurance to be taken from the initial buyer for mitigating the default risk. The dCash issuing company may also take collateral considering the nature of risk.

(iii) Risk: It will require large investment for developing web-based secure and user-friendly software.

Risk Mitigation: There will be an opportunity to become a pioneer in this sector. Moreover, our plan will help develop user-friendly and secure software easily.

(iv) Risk: Customer is not habituated to this system.

Risk Mitigation: This is a new system but customers are habituated to technology in different forms like smart phone and internet. As such, the customers can easily adapt to the proposed system.

(v) Risk: The maximum loan amount is not mentioned here.

Risk Mitigation: In this case, the bank/fintech company will provide points instead of cash credit. However, the maximum point can be equivalent of 90 per cent of receivable value (bill value).

(vi) Risk: Risk of Technology Operation like hacking, etc.

Risk Mitigation: The proposed dCash will be utilized only under a single application (app). As such, no chance is there to transfer the fund to any other network.

Finally, the proposed Digital Cash (dCash) system will support business enterprises, financial institutions, and government agencies by improving working capital efficiency, enhancing transparency in commercial transactions, strengthening revenue collection, and contributing to sustainable economic growth and thus overall economic development.

The author is a banker.

item.title: What if Ganges Water Treaty is not renewed
item.description:
By Muhammad Nawshad Zamir

Thirty years is a long time for any treaty to hold. The Ganges Water Sharing Treaty, signed on December 12, 1996 in New Delhi, has quietly governed how much dry-season water reaches Bangladesh for three decades. It survived governments of both signatory countries. The treaty ends on December 12, 2026. Talks on what replaces it are underway in Dhaka and New Delhi, but talks and treaties are not the same thing, and there is no guarantee the second will exist by the time the first anniversary arrives.

It is thus worth asking, calmly and now, rather than in a panic come December -- what happens if it doesn't'? Does Bangladesh simply lose its claim to the river, and hope India feels generous? It's a fair worry. Roughly forty per cent of the country's people depend, one way or another, on what the Ganges offers them each dry season; irrigation, drinking water, fisheries, a coastline that salt water hasn't yet swallowed. But the worry rests on a misunderstanding of how international law actually works. A treaty is not the only mechanism standing between an upstream state and an unchecked hand on the tap. There is a body of law underneath it, one that applies whether or not any two governments have bothered to sign anything.

An old argument, long settled

In 1895, the American Attorney General (in Bangladesh terms the law minister) Judson Harmon, arguing with Mexico over the Rio Grande, put forward the idea that a country could do exactly as it liked with water flowing through its own soil; the consequences or repercussions downstream be damned. It is a seductive argument if you happen to be in the upstream. And for a while this macho doctrine had followers. It does not have any left. No court of good standing has ever upheld it and no serious government defends it today. Even the United States within a decade abandoned this position and negotiated a water sharing deal with Mexico instead, for whatever its worth. The opposite argument or extreme that a downstream county can demand the river's flow, untouched, forever, collapsed just as quickly for the obvious reason that it would leave upstream states unable to build so much as an irrigation canal.

What survived and what actually governs today, is somewhat in between. States sharing a river keep their sovereignty over the water within their own territory, but that sovereignty comes with strings attached, use it reasonably, and don't wreck it for the neighbours. This isn't a theory dreamed up by academics. The Permanent court of International Justice (PCIJ) said as much in 1929, ruling that an international river creates a "community of interest" among the states that share it, a shared stake that no single riparian gets to override (Territorian Jurisdiction of the International Commission of the River Oder). This laid down the groundwork for modern customary international law. An arbitral tribunal echoed similarly in 1957 in a dispute between France and Spain over a lake in the Pyranees -- an upstream state doesn't need the downstream state's permission to build, but it does have to consult honestly, in good faith and actually listen.

What the world court has ruled

The clearest word on this comes from the International Court of Justice (ICJ) itself in a 1997 case between Hungary and Slovakia over a dam on the Danube. The court held that every state sharing a river is entitled to "an equitable and reasonable share" of it. The ICJ made it clear that it is just not a matter of what a particular treaty happens to say, but a rule of international law generally. Thirteen years later, ruling on a dispute between Argentina and Uruguay over a paper/pulp mill, the court went a step further. It stated that any state planning works that could seriously affect a shared river now has to carry out a proper environmental study and notify its neighbour before going ahead (Construction of pulp mill near Fray Bentos 2010). In 2015, in a border dispute between Costa Rica and Nicaragua regarding construction of a road over the San Juan river, the Court confirmed the same duty again. This is thus not a fringe legal theory. It is what we call the world court keeps saying, case after case, decade after decade.

A warning from the Indus

If anyone doubts these rules matter, look next door. The Indus Water Treaty of 1960 between India and Pakistan is the closest example South Asia as to a model of water diplomacy. This treaty held through two wars and endless political hostility, and when India and Pakistan genuinely disagreed over a hydroelectric project on the Kishenganga, they did not rattle sabres. They went to arbitration at the Hague, which in 2013 set a minimum flow India had to guarantee downstream. Both sides accepted it. For decades, that treaty was cited around the worked as proof that even hostile neighbours can manage a shared river through law rather than force.

Then in April 2025, after the Pahalgum incident, casing death of 26 civilians in India administered Jammu-Kashmir, India put the treaty "in abeyance". This was never done before even in the midst of outright wars between the countries. India has held that line through 2026 brushing aside or ignoring a fresh arbitral ruling against them. Whatever one makes of the underlying dispute, the lesson for Dhaka is blunt: a treaty's age and reputation are not guarantee of its survival. Bangladesh should plan for the Ganges relationship with clear eyes -- not comfortable assumptions.

Where this leaves Bangladesh

None of this is an argument for easing up on the push for renewed treaty -- quite the opposite. A proper agreement, with an updated flow formula, joint monitoring and a real dispute resolution mechanism, beats reliance on general legal principles every time. Customary law is real. However, it is broad by nature and broad rules are harder to enforce in a specific dispute than a number written into a treaty. Renewal , on terms that reflect today's hydrology rather than data from the 1950s through the 1980s, should stay Dhaka's top priority. This must dominate their minds through the Joint River Commissions, and at the highest political level.

However, even if December comes and goes without a signed successor, Bangladesh is not left with nothing. India remains bound, under the customary international law and the principles of the International Court of Justice itself has repeatedly affirmed, to use the Ganges reasonably, to avoid causing serious harm to Bangladesh's own use of the river, to notify and consult before undertaking any new works that would affect its flow, and to carry out a proper environmental assessment first. These are not favours India might choose to extend. They are legal obligations. And Bangladesh should say so clearly, repeatedly and everywhere it has a voice including the UN General Assembly. From now through December, and beyond if it must.

A river does not read treaties. It rises and falls according to decisions made far upstream, regardless of what is written on paper. However, the states that share it remain bound by law all the same, treaty or no treaty. Between now and December, Bangladesh has to remain focussed on two issues, if I may put it in that way -- negotiate hard for a fair renewal and make it unmissable to India, and its rights to the Ganges water were never written entirely in the ink of 1996.

Muhammad Nawshad Zamir is a Member of Parliament and a Barrister-at-law.

item.title: Bangladesh-India trade needs a boost
item.description:
By Asjadul Kibria

Despite strained relations for more than the last two years, bilateral trade between Bangladesh and India is very much on, if not growing. The visit of a delegation from the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) last week signalled that businesses in both countries want to move ahead as far as trade is concerned. Business leaders of both countries have agreed to form business-to-business (B2B) task forces to address trade and investment barriers and strengthen bilateral economic ties. It is for the first time since the fall of Hasina's autocratic regime on August 5 2024, a high-level Indian business delegation visited Bangladesh. 

CII is one of the premier apex trade bodies in India. Established in 1895 as the Engineering and Iron Trades Association (EITA) by five firms, it became CII in 1992. The CII delegation met senior ministers and policymakers of Bangladesh, as well as counterparts. To some observers, it is an effort to break the ice so that businesses of both countries can resume reciprocal exchanges and work together to remove trade barriers.

Since the ouster of Hasina regime in a student-led mass uprising two years ago, bilateral relations deteriorated significantly. New Delhi imposed several trade barriers during the Yunus-led interim regime. Dhaka also retaliated on a limited scale. India was reluctant to accept the changed reality in Bangladesh and began exerting various forms of pressure on the interim government. For example, India cancelled the transhipment facility granted to Bangladesh for third-country exports using Indian sea routes and airports. It also imposed restrictions on imports of certain products, including ready-made garments (RMG) from Bangladesh, primarily to India's north-eastern states via land routes. India has also moved to impose anti-dumping duties on more Bangladeshi products.

All the Indian moves to impose non-tariff barriers (NTBs) are mostly linked to the ouster of the Hasina regime, New Delhi's closest ally for more than 15 years. During that period, she gradually turned Bangladesh into a subservient country by compromising foreign and trade policies in favour of New Delhi. At the same time, anti-Indian sentiment intensified, which was a critical factor in the July mass uprising. To suppress the movement, the autocratic regime used brutal force, killing 1,400 people in three weeks. More than 20,000 were injured. Nevertheless, Hasina was forced to resign on August 5 2024 and flee to New Delhi for shelter. Since then, the two countries have passed through a series of diplomatic and trade rows. 

Despite all these negative developments, bilateral trade in goods increased modestly in the last fiscal year (FY26) by 13 per cent after a small growth of 6.35 per cent in FY25. Official statistics showed bilateral trade reached its highest level of $15.68 billion in FY22, then dropped sharply by 26 per cent to $11.62 billion in FY23. It declined by a further 9 per cent to $10.60 billion in FY24. Thus, the decline in bilateral trade was evident before the July mass uprising.

Exports to India were almost stagnant at $1.76 billion in the last fiscal year, down from $1.77 billion in FY25. Imports from India jumped 15 per cent to $10.96 billion in FY26 from $9.47 billion in FY25, widening the trade gap with India to $9.20 billion from $7.70 billion.

The bilateral trade gap is nothing new, as Bangladesh imports more products from India as raw materials, intermediate goods, and consumer products. As the next-door neighbour with extensive road, rail, and water networks, sourcing from India is generally less expensive. For Indian exporters, Bangladesh is a lucrative market with increasing consumer demand, and it is the seventh-largest export destination for India. 

Investment from India declined significantly, reflecting the strained bilateral relations. Net inflow of Indian FDI increased to $132.83 million in FY23 from $72.34 million in FY22, then declined to $105.81 million in FY24. During the first nine months of FY26, net FDI from India stood at $87.60 million. Bangladesh's internal condition was also not adequately supportive of foreign investment as the country had to allow the dust of July 2024 uprising to  settle. In the context of CII delegation's visit, a few trade analysts [www.fashionunited.uk] pointed out that for Bangladesh the challenge is less about becoming cheaper than about remaining attractive enough to clothing manufacturers who will be willing to continue investing there. For India, it is about deciding whether its neighbour should remain primarily a deficit market or become more of an extension of its own textile industrial base. 

As India stopped issuing tourist visas for almost two years, tourist arrivals from Bangladesh to India declined sharply. According to the Indian Tourism Ministry, about 2.12 million Bangladeshi tourists visited India in 2023. It declined by 17 per cent to 1.75 million in 2024 and dropped further by 73 per cent to 0.43 million in 2025, causing a significant loss of revenue for the Indian tourism industry.  The tourist visa is finally opened two months back. 

All these statistics show that the two countries are strongly linked economically. Disruption of this link by imposing trade restrictions will not work. Instead, it is better to accept the changed reality and enhance trade cooperation. India needs to respect the verdict of the people of Bangladesh and should not interfere in the latter's internal affairs. It must clearly acknowledge that no 'vassal state' type bilateral relationship is possible. Despite having strong leverage to put Bangladesh in geo-political trouble, it is not a good option for New Delhi to ignore the ground reality. There should be a win-win bilateral trade relationship.

India Brand Equity Foundation (IBEF), an entity established by the Indian commerce and industry ministry, noted recently that bilateral ties 'today reflect a more mature and diversified partnership that goes well beyond conventional areas of engagement.' It added that though tourism, healthcare, and education continue to anchor people-centric cooperation, with Bangladesh remaining a key source of inbound tourists for India, bilateral collaboration is increasingly shaped by technology and sustainability-led priorities. To what extent this cooperation will be extended in the near future largely depends on New Delhi's goodwill.
item.author: Asjadul Kibria

item.title: Improvised engine boats are invitation to mishap
item.description:
By Atiqul Kabir Tuhin

The recent capsizing of a passenger-carrying engine boat near Sabdi Ghat in Sonargaon upazila of Narayanganj, which left dozens of passengers drifting in the river before they were rescued by another boat, once again exposes the vulnerability of travelling on engine boats. Accidents on rivers, like road accidents, have become a recurrent tragedy. Owing to sustained campaigning and efforts to improve safety, launch journeys have become relatively safer, with fewer major launch accidents reported in recent years. But while safety gap was plugged on one side, another gap was created on another side. The so-called engine boats that lack scientific design, proper safety standards or trial runs, have emerged as a menace on the country's waterways.

The engines used in most of these boats are not meant for use in boats. The contraption is actually an improvised one. Shallow pump engine for use in irrigation is fitted to ordinary boat to make this so-called engine boat. One may appreciate the innovativeness of the people for crafting such a vessel but as its design does not follow any standard engineering practice necessary to build a watercraft, its safety aspects remain a big concern. Consequently, engine boats have become more accident-prone than any other water vessels. The risk is accentuated because of overloading and reckless riding. Worse yet, amateurs, minors are often found operating them. With little to no inspection and monitoring, their use is growing unchecked, and one fatal mishap is followed by another. 

The number of engine-powered vessels operating in the country is estimated at around 250,000, but only about 1,500 are reportedly registered with the authorities. This means that a vast number of vessels are operating outside the formal system of inspection, registration and safety oversight. Against this backdrop, the launch of the country's first-ever nationwide vessel census on August 20 is a timely initiative to bring this rapidly growing and largely unregulated sector under proper supervision and monitoring. The Department of Shipping and the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics are conducting the census to determine the number, types, ownership and registration status of engine-powered vessels operating across the country's maritime, coastal and inland waterways.  For a country where rivers and other waterways remain an essential means of transport, enforcing effective safety regulations is a prerequisite for making them safer.

The irony, however, is that there is no dearth of laws and regulations governing water transport. Requirements concerning vessel fitness, passenger capacity, crew competency and safety equipment are already in place. The gap lies in enforcement, and the census should provide an opportunity to bring vessels under effective regulation and identify and bar unfit ones from plying. At the same time, greater emphasis must be placed on prevention. Modern navigational technologies such as radar and Automatic Identification Systems (AIS), along with proper route planning and real-time vessel tracking, can reduce risks, while adequate life jackets, lifeboats and firefighting equipment are equally vital. Ultimately, the success of the first-ever vessel census will not depend on the number of vessels counted, but by how effectively those vessels are brought under regulation and how far the exercise helps protect the millions who depend on waterways. Accidents cannot be eliminated but accidents that occur due to wilful negligence and violation of safety rules should be shown zero tolerance.

item.title: Combating rising cost of living and food insecurity
item.description:
By Muhammad Mahmood

Bangladesh's cost-of-living crisis has become one of the clearest signs of the country's deeper economic strain. Although headline inflation has eased slightly, falling from 9.42 per cent in May 2026 to 9.16 per cent in June and 8.32 per cent in July, this improvement has brought little relief to ordinary households. Food, energy, rent, transport, and utility costs remain high, while wages have failed to keep pace. For many families, the issue is no longer whether prices are rising faster, but whether incomes can cover basic needs at all.

This pressure reveals a crisis that is both economic and structural. Persistent inflation is being reinforced by import dependence, fragile supply chains, currency depreciation, weak market supervision, slow job creation, falling real wages, and governance failures rooted in patronage and rent extraction. These forces have weakened household resilience, reversed earlier progress in poverty reduction, and exposed how vulnerable Bangladesh's development model remains to domestic distortions and external shocks.

Although inflation has eased from its recent peak, Bangladesh remains far from a stable price environment. Food inflation fell from 8.60 per cent in June to 7.16 per cent in July 2026, but prices remain high enough to place serious pressure on low-income households. Moreover, the official data produced by the Bangladesh Bureau of Statistics may not fully reflect conditions on the ground. World Economics has raised concerns about the reliability of Bangladesh's GDP, growth, and demographic data, as well as derived indicators such as GDP per capita and debt per capita that depend on government-produced economic statistics.

Non-food inflation also remains elevated, especially in housing, utilities, transport, health, and education. For households already spending much of their income on essentials, even slower price increases offer limited relief because the overall price level remains permanently higher.

Bangladesh Bank's recent 50-basis-point cut in the policy lending rate to 9.5 per cent signals a move away from aggressive tightening towards support for economic recovery. However, lowering rates while inflation remains high could add further price pressure. Monetary tightening has also had limited effect because inflation is not driven by demand alone. Supply-chain constraints, weak market oversight, money laundering, smuggling, and higher domestic prices for electricity, gas, and petroleum have all helped keep inflation persistent.

Bangladesh has a large agricultural sector, yet it remains structurally dependent on imports for several key staples and production inputs. This import intensity makes domestic prices highly sensitive to global trade shocks, freight disruptions, exchange-rate depreciation, and geopolitical conflict. Essential imports include wheat, edible oils, sugar, maize, fuel, and raw materials for the ready-made garment sector.

Wheat illustrates this vulnerability. Despite strong domestic rice production, local wheat production covers only a small share of total demand. Bangladesh has relied heavily on foreign suppliers, including Russia and Ukraine, and the Russia-Ukraine war disrupted a substantial portion of its wheat imports. India's export restrictions added further pressure, forcing Bangladesh to diversify suppliers and exposing how quickly external shocks can raise domestic food costs.

The broader import bill reinforces the same pattern. Merchandise imports reached roughly $71.14 billion in FY2025-26, driven by raw materials, refined petroleum, mineral fuels, and food grains. With China and India serving as major sources, any depreciation of the taka directly raises the local cost of fuel, food, and industrial inputs.  

The effect on poverty has been severe. National poverty is estimated to have risen back towards roughly 21 to 28 per cent after years of economic shocks, stagnant employment growth, and sustained inflation. Nearly one-third of the population lives just above the poverty line with little savings, making them highly vulnerable to rising food, fuel, rent, and transport costs.

Real wages have not kept pace with inflation. As prices rise faster than income, vulnerable households are forced to devote more than half of their daily spending to food alone. This leaves less money for healthcare, education, housing quality, transport, and nutritional diversity. The result is not only lower consumption, but also a worsening of long-term human development outcomes.

Food insecurity has become one of the clearest signs of this pressure. An estimated 15.5 million people struggle to afford basic meals, while many of the poorest families remain outside effective social safety nets. The problem is intensified by climate disruptions, rising energy costs, weak employment growth, and limited public protection for households facing repeated shocks.

The labour market has weakened alongside rising living costs. Job creation has slowed in both formal and informal sectors, putting particular pressure on urban households, young people, women, and prime-age workers. Official unemployment figures also understate the problem because they do not fully capture underemployment, discouraged workers, or unstable informal jobs.

Weak wage growth also makes consumption-led recovery fragile. If ordinary workers are losing purchasing power, household demand cannot sustainably drive growth. Any consumption gains are more likely to come from higher-income households with access to assets, savings, capital income, or stock-market gains. That creates an economy that may appear stable in aggregate while remaining deeply unbalanced for low- and middle-income families.

Bangladesh's external accounts show both resilience and fragility. Remittances reached a historic high of about $35.6 billion in FY2025-26, providing an important cushion for foreign-exchange stability. At the same time, the trade deficit widened to more than $27.3 billion as imports rose and export growth remained weak. The current-account deficit remained manageable, but foreign-exchange reserves and the value of the taka remain central to the cost-of-living outlook.

The depreciation of the taka raises the domestic price of imported fuel, raw materials, and food grains. This is why inflation in Bangladesh cannot be understood only through domestic demand: it is also shaped by the country's dependence on imported essentials and its exposure to global financial and commodity-market conditions.

The cost-of-living crisis is also tied to governance. Competitive clientelism describes a political system in which rival parties or elites compete for power by distributing state resources, jobs, contracts, and favours through patronage networks. Instead of building broad public policy around national welfare, political actors often use targeted rewards to secure loyalty and maintain influence.

In Bangladesh, this form of politics has weakened public institutions, distorted market supervision, and allowed rent-seeking networks to influence economic life. Under Sheikh Hasina, competitive clientelism increasingly merged with authoritarian control and criminalised patronage, deepening public frustration. The July 2024 uprising that removed her government reflected not only opposition to repression and corruption, but also rejection of an entrenched political order that had failed to protect ordinary citizens from economic insecurity.

The incoming government faces a difficult task. It must manage inflation, rebuild confidence, strengthen social protection, improve market oversight, and recalibrate economic policy while navigating regional geopolitical pressures. If patronage networks simply change hands rather than being dismantled, the structural causes of poverty and inflation will remain unresolved.

Bangladesh's rising cost of living and renewed poverty cannot be explained by inflation alone. They stem from interconnected pressures, including dependence on imported essentials, currency depreciation, weak wage growth, limited job creation, fragile safety nets, and governance failures that have allowed market distortions and rent-seeking to persist. Although headline inflation has begun to fall, ordinary households will not feel real relief unless prices stabilise, incomes recover, and basic goods become more affordable. A lasting response therefore requires more than short-term monetary adjustments. Bangladesh needs stronger domestic production, better market oversight, fairer labour-market outcomes, wider social protection, firm action against illicit financial flows, and a political settlement that puts public welfare ahead of patronage and private gain. Without these reforms, people living in poverty-one of the main drivers of food insecurity-will remain vulnerable to every new shock, while economic recovery will continue to exclude those who need it most.
